title: Yoga (revisited)
hook: follow any line of teachers back far enough and you meet a question: who taught the first one?

segments.voice: Yesterday Yoga closed the week with a turn: when a harmful thought arrives, follow it to where it leads, and cultivate the opposite. Did a sharp reply get a second look? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

Who taught your teacher? It's a fair question in any craft. A violinist learned from someone, who learned from someone, who learned from someone else. Earlier this season the Samkhya Karika told its own chain: Kapila, then Asuri, then Panchashikha, and on down to Ishvarakrishna. Every link is a person who was once a beginner. But keep climbing back up any line like that and you hit a strange question at the top. Who taught the first one? Patanjali's Yoga Sutras give an answer, and it's a clear place to see how Yoga parts ways with its closest neighbor.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOUR TEACHER?` → `THE CHAIN OF NAMES.` → `WHO TAUGHT THE FIRST?`

segments.voice: Three days ago, Ishvara came up in a single line, as one of the two things Yoga adds to Samkhya's map. Today we stay with it. Stillness can come, Patanjali says, through devotion to Ishvara, the Lord. Then he says who Ishvara is, and he uses Samkhya's own vocabulary to do it. Ishvara is a particular purusha, a witness like the others, but one never touched by the afflictions, by actions, by their ripening, or by the traces they leave. Remember the many purushas the Karika argued for, each of them seeming caught up in the world's show until the seeing is complete. Ishvara, in Yoga, is the one who was never caught. Then the line that answers the hook. Ishvara, the sutra says, is the teacher of even the earliest teachers, because Ishvara isn't limited by time. At the top of every chain of teachers, Yoga places one who never had to be a beginner. And Patanjali gives a way to reach toward him: his word is Om. Repeat it, the sutras say, and dwell on its meaning. Some readers call Yoga the Samkhya with Ishvara, and that's a fair label for the difference. Samkhya's count, as we heard it, had no place in the list for a Lord. Yoga keeps the list and adds one witness above the chain. Hindu tradition lets both schools stand side by side, and asks neither one to step down.
screen: `THE SAME MAP, A PRACTICE ADDED.` · `A PURUSHA NEVER CAUGHT.` · `TEACHER OF THE EARLIEST TEACHERS.` · `HIS WORD IS OM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor the chain for two minutes. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one person who taught you something that stuck. A parent, a coach, a friend. Then the person who taught them, if you know. Let the line run back as far as it goes, and rest at the top of it, wherever that is for you. If you pray, you can say Om quietly a few times, as the sutras describe, and dwell on what it means to you. The bell holds the time.
Yoga. The school that keeps Samkhya's map and adds Ishvara, a purusha never caught, the teacher of even the earliest teachers.

Your line: Yoga, revisited. Today, when you use something you were taught, a recipe, a habit, a way of saying sorry, think for one breath of the chain of people it came down through. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, devotion to Ishvara is offered as one way toward stillness, and practitioners who follow it may repeat Om and reflect on its meaning, as the sutras describe.

fork.setup: you're a student of Yoga, tracing your teacher's teacher back as far as it goes. who does Patanjali put at the top of the chain?
options: Ishvara, the teacher of even the earliest teachers
no one: the chain has no top
fork.reveal: Ishvara. the sutras say he is the teacher of the earliest teachers, because time doesn't limit him.

original.note: Sanskrit: the Lord; in the Yoga Sutras, a particular purusha untouched by afflictions and actions.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yoga and Samkhya are the same school with two names.
what it means: Yoga keeps Samkhya's map and adds Ishvara, the purusha never caught, whose word is Om.
what a scholar hears: Yoga Sutras 1.23–1.27, where Ishvara is described in Samkhya's own terms; some readers call Yoga the Samkhya with Ishvara.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 1.23 (or by devotion to Ishvara)
Yoga Sutras 1.24 (Ishvara a particular purusha untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruition and residues)
Yoga Sutras 1.26 (teacher even of the ancients, not limited by time)
Yoga Sutras 1.27–1.28 (his expression is the pranava, Om; its repetition and contemplation of its meaning)

notes: 'Later tradition sometimes calls Yoga the Samkhya with Ishvara' (seshvara samkhya): a fact about the tradition, not stated in the sutras. Keep, soften or cut.
'Samkhya's count, as we heard it, had no place in the list for a Lord' refers to what this path taught last week; confirm it doesn't overstate the Karika's position.
The practice offers Om only 'if you pray'.
Ishvara and Om were taught verse by verse in year two (days 436–437); this day's angle is the difference between Yoga and Samkhya.

Editor: 'last week' corrected (the Karika's lineage was day 1176, two weeks back); superlative 'the clearest place' softened; the many purushas now 'seeming caught', since day 1180 taught that the witness was never really bound; 'later tradition calls' changed to 'some readers call' (claims rule) in teach and trapdoor.
